chapter: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
title: Hammer hardness and tone on xylophone and vibes
summary: He explains why he plays with half-hard hammers and why striking harder only shatters the sound, especially on microphones.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Well I guess there was always a big emphasis on attack, was there, Red?
There was always a big emphasis on attack, they're drummers. ... I suppose for those guys -- (unintelligible).
Well there's a difference between lob -- attack doesn't always have to be loud -- you know?
I mean I played -- I never played with those loud hammers, that they used --
I always played with half hard hammers.
I felt that there was always -- there was a pinnacle -- the volume that you could get out of anything.
I really think that's the way it was with vibes, too. I think there's only so much sound that you get --
No matter how hard you hit them --
-- it will only vibrate to a certain degree. But vibes over that, it's going to shatter.
And I felt that was it. Of course, xylophones won't take a hard hammer better.
But that's a different metallic sound.
So I found with a half hard hammer I could get -- get what I wanted.
And with the mike in a radio station --
